title: Client-Server Systems, RPC, REST and Message Queues
objectives: Describe the client-server request/response lifecycle including connection setup costs
Explain how RPC hides network calls behind function-call syntax and why timeouts create ambiguity
Classify HTTP verbs by safety and idempotence and choose status codes that convey outcome
Compare synchronous RPC against message-queue-mediated communication using latency, coupling and load-shaping criteria
Compute queue backlog growth from producer/consumer rates and size a consumer to drain it in a target time
motivation: A trading application is never one program: an order router calls a risk service, a blotter publishes fills, a reporting job consumes everything asynchronously. The dominant architectures for that wiring. RPC frameworks, REST APIs and message queues, differ in latency, coupling and failure behaviour, and picking the wrong one shows up as p99 latency spikes or lost fills. This lesson builds the vocabulary and the arithmetic you need to reason about those choices before you ever wire one up.

blocks.text: The client-server model, end to end

blocks.md: In this simplified cold HTTP-over-TCP example, count uncached DNS separately, one RTT for TCP, two RTTs for a full TLS 1.2 handshake and one RTT for request/response, plus processing and transfer time. At0.5 ms RTT that is 1.5 ms of TCP/TLS setup before a0.5 ms request round trip. TLS 1.3, resumption, multiplexing and HTTP/3 have different handshake/transport behaviour. Pooling can amortise setup while a connection stays usable; it does not remove every DNS or reconnection cost.

rows: the real work, budget for it explicitly

blocks.text: RPC: the network disguised as a function call

blocks.md: **Remote Procedure Call** frameworks such as gRPC let you call `get_quote(ticker)` on another machine as if it were a local function. Generated **stubs** on each side handle **marshalling**, packing arguments into bytes on the wire (via a schema such as Protocol Buffers) and unpacking the reply. The convenience hides a brutal truth: a local call either runs or crashes your process, while a remote call has a third outcome. If the client times out, it cannot tell whether the server (a) never received the request, (b) executed it but the reply was lost, or (c) is still working. The **failure ambiguity** is unavoidable, the network cannot prove a negative, and it dictates the design rule of the next lesson: make repeated execution of the same request harmless (idempotence), because timeouts force retries.

blocks.title: Timeout does not mean failure
blocks.md: A timed-out order request may still land. Blindly retrying can double-submit an order; blindly giving up can orphan a fill. Distinguish *unknown outcome* from *known failure* in your code paths, this single distinction drives idempotency keys, deduplication and reconciliation systems.

blocks.text: REST: resources, verbs and status codes

blocks.md: Resource-oriented APIs commonly use HTTP semantics. GET is safe in intended effect, although incidental logging may occur. PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating an identical request has the same intended effect, not necessarily the same response. POST is not guaranteed safe or idempotent, but an application can add idempotency keys. Status codes guide rather than fully determine retries: unchanged malformed 400 requests should be fixed,429 may require waiting per Retry-After, and 503 may be transient. Retry only within a bounded policy that checks operation safety, unknown outcomes and application guarantees.

blocks.text: Message queues: communication with a buffer

blocks.md: A broker or log can buffer messages between producers and consumers. A producer need not wait for consumer processing, but it may wait for broker acknowledgements, durable replication or available buffer space. Availability, durability, ordering, replay and duplicate delivery depend on the product and configuration. Kafka retention can permit replay; a consumed/deleted queue message is not automatically replayable. At-least-once processing needs duplicate-safe consumers. Neither queues nor RPC eliminate failure coupling: the broker itself can be unavailable or throttled.

blocks.title: Worked example: backlog arithmetic
items: Producer (market-data publisher): 1{,}200 messages per second. Consumer (feature extractor): 1{,}000 per second.
Deficit: $1200 - 1000 = 200$ messages per second accumulate in the queue.
After 60 seconds: $200 \times 60 = 12{,}000$ messages of backlog, and latency to consume a 'fresh' message grows by $12000/1000 = 12$ seconds.

With producers continuing at 1,200/s, draining 12,000 messages in60 seconds needs net drain 200/s, so total consumer capacity must be1,200+200=1,400/s. Capacity 1,200/s only stops further growth; the backlog never drains. If producers stop,200/s alone drains it in60 seconds.

blocks.code:
produced_per_s = 1200
consumed_per_s = 1000
backlog = 0
for _ in range(60):                 # one minute of steady overload
    backlog += produced_per_s - consumed_per_s
print(backlog)                      # 12000
print(backlog / consumed_per_s)     # 12.0 seconds of added latency
blocks.caption: Starting empty under constant rates, backlog grows to 12,000 messages in60 seconds. At1,000/s service this is approximately 12 seconds of queue work, not minutes. Arrival/service timing and scheduling affect individual message latency.

blocks.title: Backlog is stale data
blocks.md: A12,000-message queue represents work waiting for service. At1,000/s it is about 12 seconds of queued work under a simple FIFO fluid model. Whether those messages are obsolete depends on event timestamps, processing policy and the application; queue depth is an alert signal, not proof that every computed feature or signal is wrong.

blocks.caption: Illustrative normalised M/M/1 waiting-time shape: rho/(1-rho), with utilisation rho in[0,1). Under that specific stable queue model, waiting time in units of mean service time grows sharply near full utilisation. General queue delay depends on arrival and service variability, capacity and scheduling; the curve is not a guarantee for every queue.

blocks.md: Use **RPC/REST** when the caller needs the answer now, order validation, position checks, pricing requests. Use a **queue** when the requester does not need to block: order *events* to the blotter, ticks to analytics, end-of-day jobs. A production trading stack uses both: synchronous paths for anything that gates an order, queue-backed paths for everything downstream. The failures differ too. RPC couples availability (if the risk service is down, orders stall), while a queue converts downtime into delay, bounded only by buffer capacity and consumer throughput.

guidedExercise.prompt: A risk-check service is called over RPC by the order gateway. Each call's server processing takes 4 ms; the network RTT is 1 ms; on a cold connection the client also pays DNS (0.5 ms), TCP handshake (1 RTT) and a TLS 1.2 handshake (2 RTT). (a) Compute the total latency of a cold first call. (b) Compute the latency of a call on a warm, pooled connection. (c) The gateway makes 200 cold calls per second. How much time per second is spent on setup alone, and what would pooling save?
hints: Setup stages each cost round trips; RTT is 1 ms here.
Setup cost per cold call times 200 gives the per-second waste.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Setup: DNS 0.5 + TCP $1 \times 1$ + TLS $2 \times 1$ = 3.5 ms; plus request RTT 1 ms; plus processing 4 ms. Total $= 3.5 + 1 + 4 = 8.5$ ms. (b) Warm: request RTT 1 ms + processing 4 ms $= 5$ ms. (c) Setup waste per cold call is $3.5$ ms, so 200 cold calls burn $3.5 \times 200 = 700$ ms of aggregate per-request setup latency each second, a fully reusable pooled connection can avoid that setup in this model; concurrent waits overlap, so this is not necessarily 700 ms of elapsed wall-clock or CPU time; per call that is a 41% latency reduction (8.5 to 5 ms).
guidedExercise.successCheck: Cold latency 8.5 ms and warm 5 ms under the specified TLS 1.2 model. Setup sums to 700 ms of aggregate request latency per second, not necessarily elapsed wall-clock time.

independentExercise.prompt: A queue fronts an EOD position-reporting service. Producers push 900 messages/s; the consumer handles 750/s for the first 2 minutes of the burst, then an autoscaler doubles consumer capacity to 1{,}500/s. (a) How many messages are queued after the 2 minutes? (b) How long does the doubled consumer take to drain the backlog (to the nearest second, assuming producers have stopped)? (c) Under a fluid FIFO approximation, how long does a message arriving immediately as scaling occurs wait behind the existing backlog, excluding its own service time? Assume producers stop then and scaling is instantaneous.
hints: Backlog accumulates at producer rate minus consumer rate.
The last-enqueued message waits for the entire backlog ahead of it.
independentExercise.solution: (a) Deficit $= 900 - 750 = 150$/s; over 120 s: $150 \times 120 = 18{,}000$ messages. (b) $18000 / 1500 = 12$ seconds. (c) In the fluid approximation, a new message sits behind about 18,000 queued messages; at the eventual 1{,}500/s rate that is $18000/1500 = 12$ seconds of wait (during the slow phase it would have been $18000/750 = 24$ seconds), this fluid-model queue wait is halved relative to maintaining 750/s after producers stop, not a general worst-case latency guarantee.
independentExercise.successCheck: Backlog 18,000; with arrivals stopped and instantaneous 1,500/s service, fluid drain time 12 seconds. If900/s arrivals continued instead, net drain 600/s would require 30 seconds.

commonMistakes: Treating a timed-out RPC as a failed one: the request may have executed, so retries need deduplication or idempotent design.
Retrying from status class alone:429 and some 408/5xx cases may be transient, but method semantics, application idempotency, Retry-After and retry budgets decide whether a retry is safe.
Reading queue depth as 'free buffering', backlog is latency, and unbounded queues end in out-of-memory crashes or stale-data decisions.
Assuming a queue guarantees exactly-once processing: at-least-once delivery means consumers must handle duplicates.
realWorldApplication: Every web and trading backend is a web of these three patterns: REST or gRPC at the edges for interactive calls, queues (Kafka especially) as the nervous system for events, and connection pools hiding protocol setup costs at every hop.
quantFinanceApplication: Order gates (risk, limit checks) are synchronous RPCs because the answer gates the order; fills and ticks flow through Kafka topics into blotters and analytics; and queue-depth monitoring is how desks detect that their downstream consumers have fallen behind the tape.
summary: Client-server requests pay fixed protocol taxes (DNS, TCP, TLS) that pooling amortises; processing time is budgeted separately from round trips.
RPC marshals calls over the wire but introduces failure ambiguity: a timeout means 'unknown outcome', forcing idempotent designs and explicit reconciliation.
GET is safe in intended effect; PUT/DELETE are idempotent, while POST is not guaranteed idempotent. Retry policy also needs application semantics and status details, not only 4xx versus 5xx.
Queues can buffer bursts and decouple processing, but broker acknowledgement/backpressure may still block producers. Backlog changes by arrivals minus actual departures and cannot fall below zero.
Sync calls gate decisions (orders); queues carry events downstream (blotters, analytics), production trading stacks deliberately use both.

quiz.prompt: An RPC client times out after 2 seconds waiting for a risk check. What is the correct interpretation of the timeout?
options: The network is definitely down and no service can be reached
The server definitely completed the check before the timeout
The outcome is unknown; the check may or may not have executed
The server definitely received nothing and no action occurred
quiz.explanation: A timeout means the reply did not arrive; the request may have been lost, executed-but-reply-lost, or still in progress. Only the outcome is unknown, which is why retries require idempotence or deduplication.

quiz.prompt: Which HTTP verbs are idempotent by specification (repeating the request leaves the same end state)?
quiz.explanation: GET is safe and idempotent in intended effect; PUT and DELETE are idempotent even if later responses differ. POST is not guaranteed idempotent by method semantics, though an application may supply a deduplicated operation using an idempotency key.

quiz.prompt: A producer emits 1{,}200 messages/s while the consumer processes 1{,}000/s. How many messages are in the backlog after 45 seconds?
quiz.explanation: Starting from an empty queue, arrivals exceed service by 1,200-1,000=200 messages/s. Over 45 seconds the accumulated backlog is 200*45=9,000 messages. This constant-rate fluid calculation assumes no drops, retries or other consumers change those rates.

quiz.prompt: Continuing from a 9{,}000-message backlog with producers stopped: how many messages per second must the consumer process to drain it in exactly 30 seconds?
quiz.explanation: $9000 / 30 = 300$ messages per second of pure drain capacity (on top of any new production, which is assumed stopped).

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
produced_per_s = 1200
consumed_per_s = 1000
backlog = 0
for _ in range(60):
    backlog += produced_per_s - consumed_per_s
print(backlog)
print(backlog / consumed_per_s)
quiz.explanation: Backlog grows by 200 per second for 60 seconds: 12{,}000 messages. Dividing by the consumption rate gives 12.0 seconds of added latency for a message that arrives at the end of the window.

quiz.prompt: Give two distinct reasons a design might route order *events* through a message queue rather than calling the blotter service synchronously over RPC.
quiz.modelAnswer: Decoupling lets the blotter be down or redeploy while a healthy broker buffers events. Load shaping lets bursts of fills wait in a buffer instead of directly overwhelming the blotter. Replay depends on broker retention, and producers can still block on acknowledgements or backpressure.
quiz.explanation: Queues buy availability independence, burst absorption and replay; the synchronous path is reserved for calls whose answer gates a decision.

quiz.prompt: Cold RPC setup has DNS 0.5 ms, TCP 1 RTT and full TLS 1.2 handshake 2 RTT. RTT is 1 ms and server work 4 ms; request/response takes one further RTT. What is total latency in ms under this model?
quiz.explanation: Add non-overlapping stages in this stated model:0.5+1+2+1+4=8.5 ms. A warm request omits the setup and takes 5 ms. Different TLS/transport versions, caching and parallelism can change real latency; the arithmetic applies to the given assumptions.

quiz.prompt: A FIFO fluid queue has 12,000 messages waiting and producers continue at 1,200/s. What total consumer rate drains the backlog in60 seconds?
quiz.explanation: Net drain must be12,000/60=200/s in addition to new arrivals. Total service therefore needs 1,200+200=1,400/s. Matching arrivals at 1,200/s prevents growth but leaves the existing backlog unchanged. If arrivals stopped, the calculation would instead use only 200/s.

quiz.prompt: Which HTTP semantics and retry statements are correct?
options: GET safety refers to intended effect, not a ban on incidental logs
DELETE can be idempotent while successive responses differ
429 can ask the client to wait with Retry-After
Every 4xx response forbids any retry under all circumstances
Every 5xx response makes an order POST safe to repeat
quiz.explanation: Safe/idempotent semantics concern intended effects. Status codes do not themselves supply deduplication: an order may already have executed despite a failed response.429 is a client-error status with an explicit waiting/retry use case, disproving the blanket no4xx-retry rule.

quiz.prompt: An order API has synchronously created a new order resource and returns its URL. Which status most specifically indicates successful creation?
quiz.explanation: 201 Created specifically indicates successful resource creation; the response can identify the new resource with Location.400 concerns a malformed request,429 rate limits and 503 temporary service unavailability. A202 Accepted would instead indicate acceptance for processing, not completed creation.

flashcards.back: On timeout the client cannot distinguish not-received / executed-reply-lost / still-running. Design rule: same request repeated must be harmless (idempotence), plus reconciliation for unknowns.
Packing structured arguments into wire bytes (per a schema like Protocol Buffers) at the caller and unpacking at the callee, the plumbing that makes a remote call look local.

GET is safe in intended effect; PUT/DELETE are idempotent; POST is not guaranteed either. Responses may vary across repetitions. Retry policy needs status details, operation semantics and bounded backoff;429 can include Retry-After.

Backlog changes by arrivals minus actual departures and stays nonnegative. FIFO fluid queue work time is about backlog/service rate. With continuing arrivals, net drain rate is service minus arrival rate.

flashcards.front: Sync RPC vs queue: when to use each
flashcards.back: RPC/REST when the caller needs the answer to proceed (order gates). Queue when the event can flow asynchronously (blotter, analytics) and you want decoupling, burst absorption and replay.
